title: Self-Supervised Keyframe Discovery for Horizon-Invariant Behavior Cloning
claim: A self-supervised three-stage procedure first learns a proxy reward, then trains a selector to pick keyframes, then trains the final policy on them.
layout: 3 numbered panels, left-to-right, rounded boxes, shared tile-stack motif
description: Three rounded panels, numbered 1 to 3 in circles at the top right and read left to right. Panel 1, Proxy Policy, shows a stack of observation tiles h_t next to a binary mask ψ_t. The masked tiles form a buffer B_t that feeds a flame-marked trainable network f_θ, which outputs the predicted action â_t, with the loss L(â_t, a_t) below. Panel 2, Selector Policy, shows a dashed yellow RL-Env box. It holds the buffer and a frozen (snowflake) f_θ* that returns a proxy reward to a trainable selector π_s. The selector sends priority actions back to the buffer. Panel 3, Behavior Cloning, shows a frozen π_s updating the buffer, which feeds a trainable π_BC that outputs â_t. Orange tiles are past frames, blue tiles are the current observation, and hatched tiles are unselected frames. Small callout labels read "random past observations" and "mnemonics".
caption: Keyframe Mnemonics three-stage training for horizon-invariant behavior cloning. (1) Proxy policy training. A random binary mask $\Psi_k$ is applied to the observation history $h_t$ to assemble a memory buffer $\mathcal{B}_t$ of size at most $k$, on which the proxy $f_\theta:\mathcal{B}\!\to\!\mathcal{A}$ is trained to predict the expert action $a_t$ under a negative log-likelihood loss $\mathcal{L}$. Combinatorial support of training data (Lemma 1) biases $f_\theta$ toward keyframe-based hypotheses (Theorem 1, Proposition 1), so the frozen objective $J_{\theta^{\ast}}(\mathcal{B}_t) = \mathcal L(f_{\theta^*}(\mathcal B_t), a_t)$ scores keyframe-rich buffers favourably (Corollary 1; Section [ref]). (2) Selector policy training. The selector $\pi_\mathrm{s}$ is trained using PPO to populate $\mathcal{B}_t$ with keyframes using $J_{\theta^{\ast}}(\mathcal{B}_t)$ as reward function (Section [ref]). (3) Behavior cloning. The trained selector is used to construct a keyframe augmented dataset $\mathcal{D}^{\dagger}$, which is then used to train the BC policy $\pi_\mathrm{BC}(a_t \mid o_t,\mathcal{B}_t)$ (Section [ref]). Throughout the figure, blue tiles denote the current observation $o_t$, orange tiles denote past frames in $h_t$, hatched tiles are frames not selected into $\mathcal{B}_t$.
abstract: Behavior cloning (BC) in non-Markovian environments is a challenging problem because policies have to reason over contextual information over long horizons. Existing policy architectures rely on recurrent or attention-based mechanisms to capture long-term dependencies. However, recurrent models suffer from hidden-state collapse and gradient instability under backpropagation through time while attention-based models are fundamentally limited by context length. To address these issues, we propose Keyframe Mnemonics, a novel self-supervised method that $\textit{discovers}$ a set of information-critical observations ($\textit{mnemonics}$) by learning an objective from randomly sampled past observations and using it as a reward for keyframe selection. We then train a BC policy that conditions on the discovered keyframes to model the action distribution. Under the simplicity bias assumption, our formulation provides context retention guarantees over an infinite horizon, while maintaining a small set of decision-relevant keyframes in the policy's working memory. We evaluate our method on synthetic memory domains, where mnemonic-conditioned BC policies achieve $100$% success rates (SR) and generalize to horizons orders of magnitude beyond training without performance degradation. Moreover, we evaluate on a memory-intensive robot manipulation benchmark, achieving a $13.9$% average absolute SR improvement over the strongest baseline across $23$ tasks. Finally, we demonstrate generalization with $80$% SR at $20\times$ longer time horizons on a real robot. Code and videos available at https://keyframe-mnemonics.github.io.
